lessons.title: What Equity Investors Expect in Return

children.text: Debt sends an invoice. On the fifth of every month the EMI leaves the bank account, and everyone in the finance team can see what the money costs. Equity sends nothing. No interest, no due date, no reminder. That is exactly why founders and managers underestimate it.
Equity has a price. It is simply charged in a currency that never appears in the profit and loss account: the return shareholders expect, and what they will do if they do not get it.

body.text: The cost of equity is not what a company pays. It is what its shareholders expect. Fail to deliver it and nobody sends a notice, but the share price falls, the next round gets harder, and eventually the people running the company change.

children.text: Different Investors, Very Different Expectations
There is no single number for what equity investors want. Expectations track risk, and risk falls sharply as a company matures.

body.caption: What equity investors expect in India

cells: Above 30% a year, accepting that most cheques return nothing
10x on a few, nothing on many
Around 30% a year at the fund level if it works
Public market investor in a listed company

body.text: Read down that last column and you have the entire logic of the funding staircase from Chapter 1. The earlier and riskier the stage, the higher the return demanded, and therefore the more of the company a given cheque buys. Cheaper equity is one of the rewards for becoming predictable.

children.text: Multiple and IRR Are Not the Same Thing
Investors talk in two languages. A multiple is simply how many times the money came back. The
internal rate of return
converts that into an annual rate, which is what actually matters, because time is the thing a fund cannot get more of.

markDefs.definition: The annual compounded return an investment delivers, taking into account how long the money was invested. Shortened to IRR.

body.caption: The same multiple is a very different result depending on how long it took
A 3x return, at two different speeds

children.text: This is why a fund approaching the end of its life behaves differently from one that has just started investing. The same exit value delivers a much weaker annual return if it arrives late, and LPs judge funds on the annual return.

body.title: Work out the multiple
body.prompt: A private equity fund invested ₹2 crore in a company and received ₹9 crore when it exited. What multiple did it make? Answer in times, for example 3 for 3x.
body.explanation: ₹9 crore divided by ₹2 crore is 4.5x. Spread over six years, that works out to about 28.5% a year, which is a strong private equity outcome. Over twelve years the same 4.5x would be roughly 13% a year, which is not.

body.title: Indicative annual return expectations by investor type (%)

body.text: The bar on the right is not an equity investor at all. It is there to show the starting point: if a 10-year Indian government security yields around 7%, nobody takes equity risk for 8%. Everything above that bar is compensation for risk.

children.text: Where the Public Market Number Comes From
For a listed company the expectation is more measurable, because there is a market price and decades of history. Long-run Nifty 50 returns give the reference point.

body.label: Nifty 50 long-run return
body.value: About 12.4% a year since inception, on a total return basis
body.context: The Nifty 50 Total Return Index, which includes dividends, has compounded at roughly 12.4% a year since its November 1995 base, and the 20-year figure is close to the same. That is the rough hurdle a listed Indian company has to clear over long periods before shareholders feel they have been paid for their risk.

children.text: Analysts build the same number from the bottom up. The
risk-free rate
is the yield on a 10-year Indian government security, which was around 7% in September 2026. On top of that sits the
equity risk premium
, commonly taken at roughly 5% to 6% for India. A company's own
beta
then scales it up or down.

markDefs.definition: The return available with effectively no credit risk. In India, the yield on a 10-year government security is the usual proxy.
The extra annual return investors demand for holding equities instead of government securities.
A measure of how much a share moves relative to the overall market. A beta above 1 means the share tends to swing more than the index.

body.caption: The capital asset pricing model, in its simplest form

body.title: Build a cost of equity
body.prompt: A listed Indian company has a beta of 1.2. Take the risk-free rate as 7.0% and the equity risk premium as 6.0%. What is its cost of equity, in percent? Answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 7.0% plus 1.2 times 6.0% is 7.0% plus 7.2%, which is 14.2%. That is the return shareholders should expect for holding this share, and therefore the minimum return the company should demand from any project it funds with equity.

body.title: Why a founder should care about a formula built for listed companies

children.text: An unlisted company has no share price and no beta, so this formula cannot be applied directly. It still matters for three reasons.
It sets the floor.
If shareholders of a listed peer expect 14%, nobody is funding your riskier private company for less.
It decides which projects are worth doing.
A project that returns 11% funded by equity costing 14% destroys value, even though the accounts show a profit.
It is what a valuer will use.
When your company is valued for a fundraise, an ESOP grant or a transfer, the discount rate in that model is built exactly this way, with extra premiums added for size and illiquidity.

Valuation mechanics are covered in the dedicated business valuation course on this platform. Here, hold on to one line: equity is not free, and 14% of your equity base is a real cost even though no invoice arrives.

Use the calculator above to feel what these rates actually do. A return of 12% against 15% looks like a small gap in a table and becomes an enormous gap over ten years. That gap is precisely what equity investors are negotiating over when they argue about valuation.
What Investors Expect Beyond the Return
Money is only part of what a company signs up for. The rest shows up every month, and founders who are surprised by it usually did not read the agreement.

body.title: What a growth investor expects vs what a mature company's shareholders expect

columns.label: A VC or growth investor in a private company
points: Aggressive growth, even at the cost of profits
Monthly or quarterly MIS within a fixed number of days
A board seat and real board discipline
Consent on key decisions written into the agreement
A credible exit path within the fund's life

columns.label: Shareholders of a mature listed company
points: Quarterly results and continuous disclosure under SEBI rules
An independent board and clean governance
Capital returned when the company cannot use it well
Liquidity, which the exchange already provides
Dividends or buybacks as a matter of policy

body.text: Notice the reversal on the last line. Early-stage investors are unhappy if you pay a dividend, because that money should be compounding inside the business. Mature-company shareholders are unhappy if you hoard cash you cannot deploy, because they can invest it better themselves. The same action is a mistake at one stage and a duty at the other.

body.title: Same multiple, different verdict
body.question: Fund A turned ₹100 crore into ₹300 crore in five years. Fund B turned ₹100 crore into ₹300 crore in ten years. Both made 3x. How should their LPs see this?
options: Identical outcomes, because the multiple is the same
Fund A performed far better, because the annual return is about 24.6% against about 11.6%
Fund B performed better, because it held longer
It cannot be judged without knowing the fees
body.explanation: Time is the whole difference. 3x in five years compounds at about 24.6% a year, while 3x in ten years is about 11.6%, which an LP could have earned from an index fund. Fees matter too, but the annual return gap here is decisive.

body.title: The invisible cost
body.question: A company funds a new project entirely with equity. The project earns a steady 11% a year. Its shareholders expect 14%. What has happened?
options: Nothing. The project is profitable, so value has been created
Value has been destroyed, because the return is below what shareholders could get elsewhere for the same risk
The company must pay the 3% shortfall to shareholders in cash
The cost of equity only applies to borrowed money
body.explanation: Accounting profit and value creation are not the same thing. Earning 11% on capital that costs 14% leaves shareholders worse off than if the company had returned the money to them. No cash changes hands, which is exactly why this destroys value quietly.

body.title: The benchmark
body.textWithBlank: Because no interest is ever charged on it, the cost of equity is best described as the return shareholders ___ rather than the amount a company pays.
body.explanation: Equity never generates a payment obligation. Its cost is an expectation, enforced through the share price, the valuation at the next round and, in the end, control of the company.

body.title: The pitch that priced itself wrong
body.scenario: You advise a Nagpur-based agri-processing company. The founder is pitching a venture capital fund for ₹20 crore, and her deck projects the business reaching ₹150 crore of revenue and ₹18 crore of profit after tax in seven years, with steady single-digit growth thereafter. She is asking for a ₹100 crore pre-money valuation and tells the fund it should be delighted with a likely 2.5x over seven years.
body.prompt: What is wrong with this pitch, and what would you advise her to do?
body.modelAnswer:
The arithmetic is the problem, not the business. A 2.5x over seven years is about 14% a year. A venture fund taking the risk of a single private, illiquid, early-stage company will not accept the return a listed index has historically delivered. It needs the possibility of 10x, because most of its other investments will return little or nothing.

There is also an internal contradiction. She is presenting a steady, moderately growing, profitable business, which is genuinely attractive, and then offering it to the one category of investor that cannot use it.

What I would advise:
1. Change the audience, not the projections. A business like this suits a growth or small-cap private equity fund, a family office, or straightforward bank debt against the new processing line. Those investors are content with 20% to 25% a year, or in the case of a lender, with 10%.
2. If she wants bank debt instead, the ₹18 crore profit and the physical assets make her a credible borrower, and she gives up no ownership at all.
3. If she still wants venture money, she has to show a path to a much larger outcome, not a higher valuation for the current plan. Funds price the size of the possible outcome, not the quality of the current business.
4. Drop the ₹100 crore pre-money from the opening conversation. A valuation asserted before the growth case is made invites a negotiation she cannot win.

The general lesson: match the investor to the return your business can realistically produce. Pitching a 14% business to a 30% investor wastes months.

body.title: Before you accept equity money, know these numbers
steps: What annual return does this investor need, and over what period?
What size of exit does that imply for our company?
Is that exit realistic for our market, or only for a different business?
What return do our existing shareholders expect, and are we beating it?
Does every project we are funding with this money clear that hurdle?
What happens to this investor if we grow steadily instead of explosively?

cards.definition: The annual return shareholders expect. Never invoiced, always real.
How many times the original investment came back, ignoring time.
The annual compounded return, which accounts for how long the money was invested.
The yield on a 10-year Indian government security, around 7% in September 2026.
The extra return demanded for holding equity over government securities, commonly 5% to 6% for India.
How much a share moves relative to the market. Above 1 means more volatile than the index.
Cost of equity equals the risk-free rate plus beta times the equity risk premium.
The minimum return a project must earn to be worth funding with that capital.

points: Equity never sends a bill, which is why its cost is underestimated. The cost is the return shareholders expect.
Expectations fall as risk falls: above 30% a year for angels and early VC, roughly 20% to 25% for private equity, roughly 12% to 15% for listed equity.
A multiple says nothing until you know the holding period. 3x in five years is about 24.6% a year, in ten years about 11.6%.
For listed companies the reference is long-run index returns, around 12.4% a year for the Nifty 50 Total Return Index since 1995.
Built from the bottom up, cost of equity is the risk-free rate plus beta times the equity risk premium.
A project earning less than the cost of equity destroys value even while showing an accounting profit.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Return expectations by investor type are indicative and vary widely. Market figures cited, including the government security yield and index returns, were accurate as reported on the dates mentioned and change continuously. Past index returns are not a promise of future returns.
